                       NEW MEXICO LARGE CUSTOMER GROUP’S
                  EXCEPTIONS TO THE CERTIFICATION OF STIPULATION

       The New Mexico Large Customer Group (“NMLCG”), pursuant to NMAC

1.2.2.20(B)(5)(b), submits the following two Exceptions to the Hearing Examiners’ Certification

of Stipulation.

                                           INTRODUCTION

       Like all good settlements, the Stipulation1 is the result of arms-length negotiation among

several sophisticated and diverse parties representing various customer interests. The Stipulation

satisfies the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission’s (“Commission”) precedent in

considering stipulations in that it: (1) resulted from serious bargaining among capable,

knowledgeable parties; (2) when viewed as a whole, benefits customers and the public interest;

and (3) when viewed as a whole, does not violate any important regulatory principle or practice.2




1
 Comprehensive Stipulation, Case No. 25-00079-UT (Jun. 22, 2026) (“Stipulation”).
2
 Case No. 25-00085-UT, Certification of Stipulation, pp. 11–12 (May 19, 2026); Case No. 20-00238-UT,
Certification of Stipulation, pp. 49–51 (Dec. 21, 2021).


                                                 1
          The NMLCG appreciates the Hearing Examiners’ recognition of the hard work and careful

balance the Stipulating Parties devoted to the Stipulation, as demonstrated by the Hearing

Examiners’ recommendation that the Commission approve the vast majority of the Stipulation.

         However, the Hearing Examiners’ recommended Stipulation modifications risk upsetting

the careful balance and trade-offs crafted by the Stipulating Parties.3 To preserve the overall

benefit of the bargain for all Stipulating Parties, the NMLCG recommends that the Commission

reject the Hearing Examiners’ recommended modifications and approve the Stipulation in whole.

In the alternative, the NMLCG asks the Commission to specifically not adopt the Hearing

Examiners’ recommended modifications addressed in the NMLCG’s two Exceptions below:

    •    Exception #1: The Commission should not adopt the second sentence in Findings of Fact
         and Conclusion of Law Section IV(9)(e)(i) which states “The system load factor used in
         the AED 4-CP method should use AED 4-CP, not the 1-CP.”

    •    Exception #2: The Commission should not adopt Findings of Fact and Conclusion of Law
         Section IV(9)(e)(iii) which states that “PTCs should be allocated with the AED 4-CP
         allocator, not the stipulated Energy-at-Source Allocator.” Adopting this provision would
         upset the negotiated balance of issues in the Stipulation and alter customers’ costs and
         credits through the Fuel and Purchased Power Cost Adjustment Clause (“FPPCAC”).

                                                      EXCEPTIONS

    •    Exception #1: The Commission should not adopt the second sentence in Findings of
         Fact and Conclusion of Law Section IV(9)(e)(i) which states “The system load factor
         used in the AED 4-CP method should use AED 4-CP, not the 1-CP.”

         The Certification of Stipulation’s recommendation to reject the Stipulation’s provision that

SPS will use a 1 Coincident Peak (“CP”) method to determine the system load factor in the

Average & Excess Demand 4 Coincident Peak (“AED-4CP”) allocation method is not supported

by the evidence and should be rejected by the Commission. Use of 1CP to determine the system



3
 The Stipulation provides the Stipulating Parties the right to withdraw from the Stipulation “If the Commission issues
an order rejecting this Stipulation or modifying one or more terms of this Stipulation in a way that is unacceptable to
one or more Signatories.” Stipulation, p. 15.

                                                          2
 load factor in the AED-4CP method was supported by evidence sponsored by several parties in

this case, including Commission Staff¸ the lone party opposing the Stipulation.4

        The Certification of Stipulation approved the use of the AED-4CP allocation methodology

for SPS production and transmission plant. The AED method allocates a portion of costs on an

average demand basis and a portion on excess demand, which is the difference between a class’s

peak demand and its average demand.5 The amount of costs allocated by the average demand is

based on the system load factor while the excess demand is measured using the 4 CPs during SPS’s

four highest demand months.6 The system load factor is the relationship between a utility’s annual

average demand and the annual peak demand. In the Stipulation the parties agreed to use 1CP to

determine the system load factor, and 4CPs to determine the difference between average and

excess demands.7

        The use of a 1 CP to determine the system load factor within the AED-4CP is well accepted

in the industry and by the parties in this case. In addition to the NMLCG,8 Walmart,9 Occidental

Permian Ltd. (“OPL”),10 and Commission Staff supported use of the 1CP to determine the system

load factor. Specifically, Staff witness Larry Blank stated in testimony:

        “For future rate cases, I recommend that the system load factor used to weight
        average demand in the average and excess demand allocation method be calculated
        using the single system peak demand, rather than the four-month average system
        peak used to compute the excess demands.”11

        The Certification of Stipulation discussed Staff witness Daren Zigich’s opposition to

Stipulation Section 1.11. However, the Certification of Stipulation correctly draws the distinction

                                                      3
 between using the 1CP for the system load factor versus the measurement of peak demands in the

AED-4CP, stating, in reference to Mr. Zigich’s testimony that:

            In considering Staff’s opposition, the Hearing Examiners first clarify that the
            change from the use of 4 peaks to 1 peak is applicable to only the system load factor
            used in the AED 4-CP method. The application of the 1-CP method to the system
            load factor does not affect the use of 4 peaks in the AED 4-CP allocation
            methodology. Hence, it is not strictly correct to state that Section 1.11 of the
            Stipulation reduces the number of peak hours from four to one. Instead, the AED
            4-CP allocation methodology still uses four peaks, but the methodology that is
            applied specifically to the system load factor is reduced from four peaks to one.12

            The Hearing Examiners’ clarification is important. The Stipulation only provides for using

a 1 CP for the determining the system load factor as part of the AED-4CP methodology and not

for measuring the peak demands, which uses 4 peaks. Therefore, the Stipulation does not reduce

the number of peaks used for measuring peak demand, nor does it conflict with the Stipulation in

Case No. 25-00085-UT, which the Certification of Stipulation correctly found.13

            Indeed, the evidence in support of using the 1CP method to measure the system load factor

in the AED-4CP, including testimony from Staff’s own witness, far outweighs any evidence in

opposition. The Commission should protect the agreement negotiated by the Stipulating Parties

and reject the Certification of Stipulation’s switch from the 1CP to the 4CP to calculate the system

load factor in the AED-4CP allocation methodology.

       •    Exception #2: The Commission should not approve Certification of Stipulation
            Findings of Fact and Conclusion of Law Section IV(9)(e)(iii) which states that “PTCs
            should be allocated with the AED 4-CP allocator, not the stipulated Energy-at-Source
            Allocator.” Adopting this provision would upset the negotiated balance of issues in
            the Stipulation and alter customers’ costs and credits through the FPPCAC.

            Substantial evidence in the record supports the allocation of Production Tax Credits

(“PTCs”) on an Energy-at-Source allocation. Altering that portion of the Stipulation will alter how



12
     Certification of Stipulation, p. 56, ¶ 150.
13
     Certification of Stipulation, p. 56, ¶ 151.

                                                     4
 costs and credits are allocated in SPS’s FPPCAC, therefore denying parties the benefit of the

bargain negotiated in the Stipulation as a whole.

         The Certification of Stipulation cites SPS’s argument and witness testimony14 explaining

why an Energy-at-Source allocator is an appropriate method to allocate PTCs. The Certification

of Stipulation also cites to extensive evidence and argument provided by NMLCG, Louisiana

Energy Services, L.L.C., Federal Executive Agencies, and OPL.15 Importantly, SPS specifically

states that “[using the Energy-at-Source Allocator] preserves SPS’s existing FPPCAC allocation

practice and avoids creating a second allocation and true-up process for the new solar PTCs.”16

         After discussing the evidence in the Certification of Stipulation, the Hearing Examiners

“see that arguments can be made for both the Stipulation’s position and Staff’s position, as SPS

has made arguments both for and against the use of the AED 4-CP allocator for the allocation of

PTCs.”17 However, the Certification of Stipulation errs by, after finding reasonable arguments

either way, upsetting the careful balance created in the Stipulation and denying Stipulating Parties

the benefit of the negotiated bargain. By altering the PTC allocation, the Hearing Examiners

replace the Stipulating Parties’ judgment for their own on one isolated issue, resulting in altered

overall rate impact to customers that is inconsistent with the Stipulation. Further, the Certification

of Stipulation does not address the necessary changes to the FPPCAC if PTCs are allocated based

on AED-4CP rather than using the Energy-at-Source allocator.

         The Hearing Examiners note that part of the reason they change the agreed allocation of

the PTCs is that “this recommendation leans in the direction of protecting non large load customers

from costs, and is a reasonable policy decision when the Commission is faced with a decision that

                                                           5
 has been argued from both sides by SPS.”18 However, the Hearing Examiners ignore that

Stipulating Parties, such as the NMDOJ, which represents small customer interests, agreed to the

Energy-at-Source PTC allocation in the Stipulation, indicating it is a reasonable give and take as

part of the overall deal.

         Unlike other portions of the Certification of Stipulation that alter the Revenue Allocation

and Rate Design portions of the Stipulation but maintain the overall base rate revenue allocation

approved by the Stipulating Parties, PTC allocation occurs through the FPPCAC where PTCs are

currently allocated on an energy basis.               This is important because, as the Certification of

Stipulation recognizes, the overall base rate revenue allocation includes significant gradualism

adjustments supporting the lower load factor and lower usage customer classes. Specifically, the

Certification of Stipulation cites to SPS witness Alexander G. Trowbridge’s testimony showing

that the Stipulation provides residential customer class gradualism support of $28.5 million.19

         Importantly, the PTC allocation will impact costs and credits that are made through the

FPPCAC and not the base rate allocation that the Commission approves in this case. Therefore,

the Certification of Stipulation directly impacts customers through the FPPCAC without making

any compensating adjustment to the base rate revenue allocation agreed to in the Stipulation. In

the overall balance of issues that were negotiated during the Stipulation process, it is possible, and

perhaps even likely, that parties may not have agreed to the proposed revenue allocation if they

were aware of a potential change to the PTC allocation in the FPPCAC.

         The Certification of Stipulation’s rejection of the Energy-at-Source PTC allocation upsets

the careful balance created by the Stipulating Parties and modifies a sole issue in isolation,

                                                           6
 resulting in different overall rate impacts than the Stipulating Parties agreed. The Commission

should reject this proposed modification that upsets the careful balance negotiated by the parties

and threatens the Stipulation as a whole.

                                         CONCLUSION

       The NMLCG respectfully requests that the Commission reject the Hearing Examiners’

proposed modifications to the Stipulation and approve the Stipulation in whole. In the alternative,

the NMLCG recommends that the Commission at least reject the Certification of Stipulation’s

modifications related to the NMLCG’s Exceptions as they are not supported by substantial

evidence in the record and deny the Stipulating Parties the benefit of the bargain negotiated in the

Stipulation.


       Respectfully submitted on November 2, 2026.
